course.title: Syrian Arabic, Start to Fluent
course.subtitle: North Levantine Arabic as spoken in Syria, from absolute beginner through fluent, everyday command
course.heroLedeSuffix: Real spoken Syrian sentences from lesson one, with transliteration and native-style audio for every line.

a1-greetings.title: Greetings: Marhaba and Kifak
a1-greetings.explanation: "مرحبا" (marhaba) is the everyday hello you'll hear everywhere in Syria — shops, taxis, cafés. "كيفك؟" (kifak, to a man) / "كيفك؟" (kifik, to a woman) asks "how are you?" — instantly recognizable as Levantine rather than textbook Arabic. The typical answer is "الحمدلله منيح" (alhamdulillah, mnih — "thank God, good"), with منيح becoming منيحة (mniha) when a woman is speaking about herself.
a1-greetings.fact: "صباح الخير" (sabah el-kheir, good morning) gets answered not by repeating it, but with "صباح النور" (sabah en-noor, literally "morning of light") — like many Arabic greeting pairs, the reply uses a different word entirely rather than echoing the greeting back.

dialogue.native: مرحبا! كيفك اليوم؟
dialogue.en: Hi! How are you today?

dialogue.native: الحمدلله منيح. وانت؟
dialogue.en: Thank God, good. And you?

a1-biddi.title: I Want: Biddi
a1-biddi.explanation: "بدي" (biddi) is the everyday way to say "I want" in Syrian Arabic — one of the most common words you'll hear. Just follow it with what you want: "بدي قهوة" (biddi ahwe, "I want coffee").
a1-biddi.fact: بدي is actually بدّ (badd-, "want/need") fused with the possessive ending "-i" (my), so it literally means something like "my wanting" — the same possessive-suffix logic that gives Arabic its other person forms of this word, though this course only teaches the widely-used 1st-person بدي form for now.

dialogue.native: شو بدك اليوم؟
dialogue.en: What do you want today?

dialogue.native: بدي قهوة اليوم، شكراً كتير
dialogue.en: I want coffee today, thank you very much

a1-present-shaf.title: Present Tense: I See, You See...
a1-present-shaf.pattern: ب- / بت- / بتي- / بي- / بت- / من- / بتو- / بي-و
a1-present-shaf.explanation: Syrian present-tense verbs take the ب- (b-) prefix plus a person marker: بشوف (bshuf, "I see"), بتشوف (btshuf, "you-m see"), بتشوفي (btshufi, "you-f see"), بيشوف (byshuf, "he sees"), بتشوف (btshuf, "she sees"), منشوف (mnshuf, "we see"), بتشوفو (btshufu, "you-all see"), بيشوفو (byshufu, "they see").
a1-present-shaf.fact: The 1st person plural "we" prefix (من mn-) looks completely different from the ب- pattern everywhere else — that's not an exception to memorize separately, it's just what happens when ب- fuses with the underlying "n-" marker for "we", a regular sound change across the whole b-prefix system.

dialogue.native: شو بتشوف اليوم؟
dialogue.en: What do you see today?

dialogue.native: بشوف بيت كبير اليوم
dialogue.en: I see a big house today

a1-fi-mafi.title: There Is / There Isn't: Fi and Mafi
a1-fi-mafi.explanation: "فيه" (fi) means "there is/are", and its negative "مافي" (mafi, from ما + فيه) means "there isn't/aren't". This simple pair is so central to everyday Levantine speech that a well-known textbook is literally named "Shou fi ma fi?" ("What's up? / What's there, what's not there?").
a1-fi-mafi.fact: "شو في ما في؟" is itself a common colloquial greeting/small-talk phrase meaning roughly "what's going on?" — literally "what is there, what isn't there" — showing how naturally فيه/مافي gets used beyond its literal grammatical meaning.

dialogue.native: في قهوة اليوم؟
dialogue.en: Is there coffee today?

dialogue.native: لا، مافي قهوة اليوم، بس في شاي
dialogue.en: No, there's no coffee today, but there's tea

a2-past-katab.title: Past Tense: I Wrote, You Saw...
a2-past-katab.explanation: Levantine past tense uses suffixes on the verb stem: كتبت (katabt, "I wrote"), كتبت (katabt, "you-m wrote"), كتبتِ (katabti, "you-f wrote"), كتب (katab, "he wrote"), كتبت (katbit, "she wrote"), كتبنا (katabna, "we wrote"), كتبتو (katabtoo, "you-all wrote"), كتبو (katabo, "they wrote"). "I" and "you-m" share the exact same form — context tells them apart.
a2-past-katab.fact: The verb شاف (shaf, "to see") follows the same suffix pattern, but as a "hollow" root (ش-و-ف) its long vowel shortens in every person except he/she/they: شفت (shift, "I saw"), شاف (shaf, "he saw"), شافت (shafit, "she saw"), شافو (shafo, "they saw") — the same aa→i shortening pattern found across hollow verbs in Arabic dialects generally.

dialogue.native: شو شفت مبارح؟
dialogue.en: What did you see yesterday?

dialogue.native: شفت بيت كبير وشفت صديق منيح
dialogue.en: I saw a big house and I saw a good friend

a2-past-negation.title: Negating the Past: Ma + Past Verb
a2-past-negation.explanation: To negate a past-tense verb, put ما (ma) right before it: ما شفت (ma shift, "I didn't see"). This is the same ما used for present-tense negation — unlike مش, which is reserved for nominal/participle sentences ("أنا مش تعبان").
a2-past-negation.fact: In fast speech, ما often contracts right onto the verb with barely a pause — ماشفت — but it's still written and thought of as two separate words, ما and شفت, not a single fused word.

dialogue.native: شفت صديق مبارح؟
dialogue.en: Did you see a friend yesterday?

dialogue.native: لا، ما شفت صديق اليوم، شفت بيت بس
dialogue.en: No, I didn't see a friend today, I only saw a house

a2-days-past.title: Days of the Week with Past Tense
a2-days-past.explanation: Combining a day name with a past-tense verb builds a simple narrative: يوم الجمعة شفت صديق (yom el-jum3a shift sadeeq, "On Friday I saw a friend"). The day name simply comes first, like a time adverb.
a2-days-past.fact: Just like مبارح (yesterday), day names need no extra preposition ("on Friday") — Syrian Arabic places time expressions directly at the start of the sentence.

dialogue.native: يوم السبت شو شفت؟
dialogue.en: On Saturday, what did you see?

dialogue.native: يوم السبت شفت بيت كبير منيح
dialogue.en: On Saturday I saw a big, good house

b1-3and.title: Possession: Andi, Andak, Ando...
b1-3and.pattern: عندي / عندك / عنده / عندا / عندنا / عندكن / عندن
b1-3and.explanation: Arabic has no verb "to have" — Syrian uses عند (3and, literally "at/by") fused with a person ending: عندي (3andi, "I have"), عندك (3andak, "you-m have"), عنده (3ando, "he has"), عندا (3anda, "she has"), عندنا (3andna, "we have"), عندكن (3andkon, "you-all have"), عندن (3andon, "they have"). Negate it with ما: ما عندي (ma 3andi, "I don't have").
b1-3and.fact: عند marks lasting/permanent possession (owning something), distinct from مع (ma3, "with") used for what you're physically carrying right now — a nuance English's single word "have" doesn't capture.

dialogue.native: عندك فلوس اليوم؟
dialogue.en: Do you have money today?

dialogue.native: أي، عندي فلوس، الحمدلله
dialogue.en: Yes, I have money, thank God

b1-lian.title: Because: Lأan and Ashan
b1-lian.explanation: لأن (la2an) and عشان (3ashan) both mean "because" and are largely interchangeable in everyday Syrian speech: أنا منيح اليوم لأن شفت الأهل ("I'm good today because I saw the family") or أنا منيح اليوم عشان شفت الأهل — either works.
b1-lian.fact: عشان also does double duty as "in order to" before a verb, not just "because" before a full clause — a small extra flexibility لأن doesn't share.

dialogue.native: ليش عندك فلوس كتير؟
dialogue.en: Why do you have a lot of money?

dialogue.native: عشان بشرب قهوة بس، ما بدي شي غالي
dialogue.en: Because I only drink coffee, I don't want anything expensive

b1plus-lazim.title: Must/Should: Lazim
b1plus-lazim.explanation: لازم (lazim, "must/should/have to") is followed by a present-tense verb: لازم بشوف الأهل (lazim bshuf el-ahl, "I must see the family"). لازم itself never changes form — only the verb that follows it conjugates for the person.
b1plus-lazim.fact: لازم can also stand alone as a short, firm reply — "لازم!" by itself means something like "You have to!" — a compact way to insist on something without a full sentence.

dialogue.native: لازم بشوف الأهل اليوم، مبارح ما شفتهم
dialogue.en: I have to see the family today, I didn't see them yesterday

dialogue.native: منيح، لازم بتحب القهوة معهم كمان
dialogue.en: Good, you should love the coffee with them too

b2-ma.title: Negation: Ma + Verb, Mish + Noun
b2-ma.explanation: ما (ma) negates a present-tense verb directly: ما بشوف البيت اليوم (ma bshuf el-beit el-yom, "I'm not seeing the house today"). مش (mish) negates a noun, adjective, or nominal sentence instead: مش منيح (mish mnih, "not good") -- verbs take ما, everything else takes مش.
b2-ma.fact: In fast, casual Damascus/Aleppo speech, ما often gets pronounced almost as a quick nasal hum fused onto the verb -- so "ما بعرف" can sound closer to "mabaaraf" than two separate words, even though it's written as two.

dialogue.native: ما بشوف البيت اليوم، مدري ليش
dialogue.en: I don't see the house today, I don't know why

dialogue.native: مش مشكلة، لازم بشوف بكرة
dialogue.en: It's not a problem, you should see it tomorrow

b2plus-lazim-ma.title: Mustn't/Shouldn't: Lazim Ma
b2plus-lazim-ma.explanation: To say someone shouldn't do something, ما slots in right before the verb, after لازم stays in place: لازم ما بتشوف هلق (lazim ma btshuf hala2, "you shouldn't see it now"). لازم itself never takes ما directly -- the negation always attaches to the verb that follows it.
b2plus-lazim-ma.fact: This exact pattern -- a fixed modal word followed by ما plus a verb -- is one of the most common ways Syrian Arabic gives advice or warnings, similar to how English speakers lean on "shouldn't" far more often than a flat "don't."

dialogue.native: لازم ما بتحب القهوة كتير هلق
dialogue.en: You shouldn't love a lot of coffee now

dialogue.native: منيح، لازم ما بشوف بيت غالي
dialogue.en: Good, I shouldn't see an expensive house

c1-chain.title: Chaining Clauses
c1-chain.pattern: الفعل + لأن + سبب + و/بس + نتيجة (verb + because + reason + and/but + result)
c1-chain.explanation: At this level, sentences stop being single statements and start chaining reason and result together: بشوف بيت جديد اليوم لأن هاد قديم كتير، وعندي فلوس منيح (I'm seeing a new house today because this one is very old, and I have good money). Each clause stays simple -- the skill is stringing 2-3 of them together fluently, the way real spoken Syrian Arabic naturally runs on.
c1-chain.fact: Long chained sentences like this are exactly how Syrian Arabic speakers naturally tell a story or explain a decision out loud -- rarely as one flat statement, almost always as a little chain of "this, because that, so this."

dialogue.native: بشوف بيت جديد اليوم لأن هاد قديم كتير، وعندي فلوس منيح
dialogue.en: I'm seeing a new house today because this one is very old, and I have good money

dialogue.native: منيح، وأنا بدي بشوف بيت الأهل لأن ما شفتهن من هلق
dialogue.en: Good, and I want to see the family's house because I haven't seen them

c2-chain.title: Four-Clause Fluency
c2-chain.pattern: الفعل + لأن + سبب + بس/و + نتيجة + و + تفصيل إضافي
c2-chain.explanation: This is the top of the course: sentences that pack four full clauses together the way a fluent speaker actually talks -- a statement, its reason, a contrast or addition, and one more detail, all in a single breath: بشوف بيت جديد اليوم لأن هاد قديم كتير، بس عندي فلوس منيح، وبدي بشوف بكرة كمان (I'm seeing a new house today because this one is very old, but I have good money, and I want to see one tomorrow too). Nothing here is new grammar -- it's the same simple pieces from the whole course, just chained at native speed.
c2-chain.fact: Reaching this level means you can follow (and produce) Syrian Arabic the way it's actually spoken in a real conversation -- not textbook sentences, but the long, looping, reason-then-detail style that native speakers use without even thinking about it.

dialogue.native: بشوف بيت جديد اليوم لأن هاد قديم كتير، بس عندي فلوس منيح، وبدي بشوف بكرة كمان
dialogue.en: I'm seeing a new house today because this one is very old, but I have good money, and I want to see one tomorrow too

dialogue.native: منيح، وأنا بدي بشوف بيت الأهل لأن ما شفتهن كتير، بس عندي شي بعدين
dialogue.en: Good, and I want to see the family's house because I haven't seen them much, but I have something later
